longformArticle.deck: A source-aware account of 1665 plague doorway warnings, St Giles enforcement, Pepys' witness account, and later threshold caution folklore.
opening: This record is centered on one tightly linked event chain in plague-era London: an official infected-house mark, a public enforcement rupture, and witnessed door warnings.
The legend form emerges only after that chain is publicly visible and repeatable, not as proof of hidden causes.

storyBody.heading: Civic orders and the visible threshold
paragraphs: The event begins with a public rule chain in plague-era London. Officials expected infected households to be isolated, and later legal instructions made that rule explicit: a suspected house was to be closed and marked on the door with a red cross and the phrase "Lord have mercy upon us." Warders were assigned to support enforcement and limit contact.

That civic order is the first concrete layer. It is not folklore yet, because the mechanism was bureaucratic: inspection, marking, access control, and penalty language. But this is the same first cause in a legend-origin chain where public instructions later become shared memory.

storyBody.heading: The St Giles incident: a marked door, then a riot response
paragraphs: On 28 April 1665, in New Buildings in St Giles in the Fields, a house was reported as suspected of plague infection, with a cross and paper fixed to its door. A court-level record shows that those marks were then removed, and the inhabitants were allowed back onto the street in disorderly fashion.
The action stage is narrow and specific:
1) the household was marked as infected, 2) the mark was publicly removed, 3) crowd pressure turned the enforcement moment into a street incident.
That sequence matters because it is one bounded event that could be repeated in memory as "what happened when the doorway warning became contested."

storyBody.heading: Eyewitness sequence: Pepys and the first visible plague signs
paragraphs: On 7 June 1665, Samuel Pepys recorded what people in the city were seeing: two or three houses with a red cross and the printed warning phrase on their doors. He described this as a first-time sight that changed the emotional state of ordinary movement through the streets.

Cause and action are visible here. The warning had moved from administration into repeated public visibility. A door sign that might have been seen as an isolated control measure was now a recognizable pattern on the urban route itself.

storyBody.heading: The doorway as warning node and household boundary
paragraphs: The same policy sequence gives the warning strong narrative force:
- A door message made risk legible from the street; - Warders and shut-up rules made that message operational; - Repeated sightings made the message portable from house to house.

Households then retained a practical lesson from this pattern: the marked door became a boundary marker of heightened danger and altered behavior. In family transmission, a public instruction can become an inherited caution phrase.

storyBody.heading: From administrative mark to folklore template
paragraphs: The strongest transformation happened after the immediate plague wave. The same format—door, short text, visible symbol, constrained movement—was later carried into moral storytelling about entrances as control points. The story form changed, but the core image remained.
That compression created a household warning template:
1) define a threshold, 2) announce caution in a short phrase, 3) treat the threshold as a memory object.
The event itself did not prove supernatural claims, but it produced a repeatable template for domestic warning language.
